title: Sliding a first-intersection cut through a homogeneous E^r run produces a new boundary inequality
statement: If the first intersection of an initial climb with a cycle lies in a homogeneous parity run, the cut may be shifted to either boundary as a first-intersection type, and choosing the peak or valley boundary of E^r produces an inequality, or a restriction on r, that is not cycleItinerary_rotateItinerary / rotateItinerary_even_run / cycle_trailing_evens_lt / even_run_scale_barrier / odd_preimage_unique / oddLanding_preimage_unique / no_cycle_itinerary_even_count_le_three / the archived OE and EO cells.
counterexamples: E|EEE, EE|EE, EEE|E are rotateItinerary of the necklace OOEEEE
100 --E--> 10 --E--> 3 versus 102 --E--> 10 --E--> 3: first intersection is 10, not the peak 100 and not the valley 3
O^r interiors are not first meetings (odd_preimage_unique); how long E^r can be is even-count plus the trailing cell
notes: Phase 0 only. Not a reopen of the E^r-block leftover-killer (that branch already pushes even interiors forward to the valley). This phase refutes the stronger bidirectional slide. Combinatorial sliding is a REPARAMETERIZATION of rotateItinerary. No finance, no K=11, no L=55293, no floor raise. No Paper A edit, no ledger row, no new Lean. Not a halt theorem.
tested_range: necklace identity at r=4; backward-slide witnesses 100 --E^2--> 3 and 10000 --E^3--> 3; trailing-cell checks 100 < 4^4 and 10000 < 4^8
